nameStory: The Green Pug gets its name from its lovely jade-green wing coloration when fresh, combined with the compact, sturdy build typical of 'pug' moths. Like a green jewel with wings, this little moth's emerald hues help it blend perfectly among the foliage where it rests during the day.
description: The Green Pug is a small, compact moth in the geometer family, known for their caterpillars that move in a distinctive looping motion. When freshly emerged, it displays beautiful green wings marked with sharp, dark bars or lines that create an intricate geometric pattern. However, this species is quite variable - some individuals appear mostly dark brown with little green showing, and the green color fades over time to duller tones. These night-flying moths are drawn to artificial lights during their summer flight period.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinct dark bars crossing green wings, with the postmedian line forming sharp, angular patterns rather than gentle curves

idTips.label: Color Variation
idTips.description: Fresh specimens show bright jade-green coloration, but older moths fade to dull green or even dark brown with minimal green visible

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Small, compact moth with a sturdy, pug-like build that feels solid if gently handled

idTips.label: Underside Markings
idTips.description: The underwing patterns are very sharply defined and contrasting when wings are spread

idTips.label: Flight Behavior
idTips.description: Active at night during June and July, readily comes to porch lights and other artificial illumination

habitat: Green Pugs are found wherever their host plants in the rose family grow, including orchards, woodland edges, parks, and gardens. Look for them near apple trees, cherry trees, hawthorns, and wild roses where their caterpillars feed on the flowers. They're equally at home in cultivated areas and semi-wild spaces throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not typically seen; the species overwinters as eggs on rose family plants, preparing for the upcoming flight season.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in June and July when adults emerge and fly at night, mating and laying eggs. This is when you'll spot them at lights or resting on vegetation during the day.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight period has ended; green caterpillars may still be found feeding on late-season flowers of rose family plants before pupating.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity; the species overwinters as eggs attached to twigs and branches of host plants, waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: Green Pug caterpillars are flower specialists that specifically target the blossoms of rose family plants - so when you see damaged apple or cherry flowers in your garden, there's a good chance these little green larvae are the culprits enjoying a floral feast!
confusionNotes: Green Pugs can be confused with other small green moths, but their sharp, angular dark wing lines distinguish them from species with gentler, curved markings. Remember: 'sharp angles for Green Pugs' - the postmedian line creates distinct zigzags rather than smooth waves.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'pug' in moth terminology refers to their compact, sturdy build rather than any resemblance to pug dogs. This moth family (Geometridae) gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'earth measurer,' referring to how their caterpillars seem to measure the ground as they loop along.
compareHints: While there are no other Pasiphila species in our New England dataset, Green Pugs can be distinguished from other small geometer moths by their combination of green coloration (when fresh) and distinctly angular dark wing markings. Most similar geometers either lack the green tones entirely or have more gently curved crosslines rather than the sharp, zigzagging patterns characteristic of Green Pugs.
